searchText: Hi. Is there any beacon chain testnet running ? Hey <@649445004250447885>, Prysmatic Labs runs one and you can join at https://prylabs.net when running the beacon chain protocol, there are certain cases when you're behind on blocks (for example during an internet outage and no peers connected) and have to figure out what to do: produce blocks, validate etc.. seemingly, the "best" thing you can do is keep running the protocol, meaning you produce for your own validators and use empty slot transitions to figure that out.. once you reconnect, you'll resync with others, start tallying and in theory, since you weren't finalizing locally, you should be able to reach a stable point by syncing with the others. here's the issue though: for how long do you replay empty blocks? eventually, the empty block processing will cause enough validators to be ejected, and things break down (because committees become empty etc). we could put an arbitrary limit on it but it would be... arbitrary. thoughts? Presently we will process skip slots for a maximum of one slot (i.e., however many slots we can skip in 12s, depends on hardware) before we return an error if two (successive) block producers are offline, you die? oh. depends on hardware. FYI I'm not claiming this is ideal, this is just what we're doing to avoid the akward lockups so you run the skip slot thing in a tight loop until 12s have passed? yep huh. interesting. adds a bit of randomness to the process across a heterogenous network 🙂 it's my version of the VDF 😛 50mil, yours or whatever the number was 🙂 i'll take 50 so on a really really really really fast machine, I can tell you it will panic: the committee will become empty and the spec is not.. written for that. we've run into this before, we throw errors in this case in those cases we had a very small validator count (my pc is not that fast 😦 ) unless I am missing something, why would you endlessly process skip slots ? wouldn't it be bound by what the current slot is because you're not receiving blocks from others because you're offline, and have to advance the state to the current slot. it's not endlessly, but potentially enough to go on for a good while (like when you restart client after a few days) or your internet is down and then comes back online, and you're not actively monitoring your node because you're busy in real life dealing with a flood, etc there's an upper bound where all validators are kicked, but it's a bit.. extreme. 1 slot of cpu time is more sane, but kind of arbitrary. I'm trying to think of any other bounds that could meaningfully be applied. gotcha, it makes sense then. This could potentially be handled by your sync protocol. If you do eventually go offline, you could notify your node through status req/resp with other peers. Ex: You were connected to 15 peers previously, and now not a single peer responds to the status request , you could probably restrict running skip slots in that case there are ways to break that: ie the first node to run the protocol will not advance because it's not connected. a single node running all validators in the network will not advance etc. why 1 connection and not 2? or 3? don't get me wrong, we'll likely end up with heuristics like that, but they're less.. satisfying 😉 no worries 🙂 I guess 1 is an arbitrary number , it could be any number that is a safe determined size. I can see that this would lead to issues especially in regards to test networks, where you have 1 node hosting all the validators. yup, or private networks etc, or headless machines that run with minimal operator involvement (embedded devices etc)
